title: House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
description: Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., appears at
body:
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., appears at a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 13, 2023. On Wednesday, he released document preservation letters that lay the groundwork for incoming investigations into the Trump family and its allies.
                
                    Drew Angerer/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Drew Angerer/Getty Images
    

   
   The highest-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee sent document preservation letters to over a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members, laying the groundwork for incoming investigations come January.   "Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become the chair of the committee. "These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning."    The California Democrat's targets fall into four broad categories: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct, and the White House Epstein cover-up."    
   "Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," many of the letters read.   The Trump administration has previously rejected accusations of misconduct and has warned Garcia that overly zealous investigations could constitute a crime — a claim legal experts have broadly pushed back against, citing Congress' oversight authorities.    In a letter dated Nov. 9, White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia the administration was "monitoring" the speech of Democrats in Congress as they mapped out investigative targets into the Trump administration. The letter warned that efforts by Democrats to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."    "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement on Wednesday in response to Garcia's letters. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."   Here's a closer look at the letters Garcia sent:    Donald Trump Jr. — "pay to play" allegations and potential conflicts of interest, his stake in World Liberty Financial, and the financing of his wedding after-party by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin.  President Trump later told reporters the costs for the wedding celebration was later paid back. "You have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father's presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people," the letter reads.  Eric Trump — "pay to play" allegations and potential conflicts of interest, his stake in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture. "Oversight Democrats have found that your roles as a co-founder of World Liberty Financial and a key player in the Trump family's pay-to-play schemes have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years," said the letter. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law — allegations of conflicts of interest, his investment firm Affinity Partners, and using his government role to enrich himself and his companies. "Directly or indirectly, you have received billions of dollars in fees and investments with particularly troubling ties to Middle East states where you also have a government role," the letter reads. "This raises urgent questions about transparency, conflicts of interest, and the abuse of what appears to clearly be a government position—with influence over war, peace, and nuclear proliferation as well as direct access to President Trump—for personal profit." Former Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle. She was previously engaged to Trump Jr., and was contacted by Garcia over allegations of pay-to-play schemes. "As ambassador, you appear to have been intent on leveraging your position to cash-in," said the letter.  Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend — construction and donations for the White House ballroom, financed in part via private donations to the Trust.  White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — allegations of abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement under his direction. "Members of the Trump Administration have described you as the 'linchpin' and 'architect' of the Trump Administration's most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties," reads the letter. "We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses."Former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski — allegations of abuse of DHS funds, corruption and self-dealing. Vice President J.D. Vance — allegations of secret meetings inside the White House Situation Room about the administration's handling of the Epstein files. "Reportedly, you were even the first to suggest that Ghislaine Maxwell be interviewed in hopes of using her testimony to distance President Trump from Epstein, despite President Trump's well-documented decades-long friendship with the notorious abuser and sex-trafficker," the letter reads. "These discussions appear to be directly linked to an apparent quid pro quo in which Maxwell was moved to a minimum-security prison camp after she made favorable statements about President Trump in a highly unusual prison interview conducted by then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche." Former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — allegations of secret White House meetings surrounding the Epstein investigation. "Reporting describes you as refusing to release documents concerning allegations against President Trump to the public," the letter said.  Attorney General Todd Blanche — allegations of a cover-up of the Epstein files, failure to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and the decision to transfer Maxwell to a minimum-security prison. "You have refused to cooperate with our investigation, or to fulfill your legal responsibilities to be transparent with the Committee and the American people," the letter said. "This obstruction is even more concerning given your direct involvement in the broader cover-up, as well as your history as President Trump's personal attorney." Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Federal Prison Camp Bryan Warden Tanisha Hall — regarding Maxwell's transfer to a minimum-security prison camp days after she was questioned about Trump and his relationship to Epstein. "Committee Democrats will not tolerate the Administration's refusal to respond to our inquiries and, in the future, will not hesitate to compel information from individuals enabling the cover-up of Maxwell's and Epstein's crimes," the letter said.

title: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
description: Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a
body:
Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference in the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.   Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.   "Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy  is a simple one. We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said after the vote.    
   Jeffries centered his remarks on cost of living issues, saying Democrats would fight to lower the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care. And in the face of what he described as "unprecedented corruption," Jeffries said Democrats would work to hold officials accountable.    "Not for partisan reasons but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," he said.    The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.   Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.   It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.   
   While Jeffries will still have to navigate intraparty divides, the size of Democrats' majority affords him room to weather some dissent.   He's faced resistance from some within the party's left-most flank, who argue Democrats should prioritize advancing a more progressive agenda next year, lobbying for votes on Medicare for All and legislation that would stop the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel.    Among those who voted against Jeffries were a number of newly-elected members — some who won with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America. In a statement after the vote, they said they have engaged in "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries to secure commitments on their policy priorities.    "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."   Among those who signed the statement were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York;  New Jersey's Adam Hamawy; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Colorado's Melat Kiros; Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.   After the vote, Jeffries told reporters "the results of today's election speak for themselves."    "We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism — not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people."     Given that Democrats will hold double digit margins in the chamber — an edge propelled by the success of more moderate candidates in districts President Trump carried in 2024 — it's unclear how much leverage the left wing of the party will have in the speaker's vote.   Divides inside the party may prove more pronounced in the Senate, where some Democrats are more publicly questioning whether current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is best suited to deliver on voter demands for change.   
   Schumer faces a challenge from Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy last week and is pitching himself as an alternative to the status quo, echoing much of the progressive populist messaging that several successful Senate candidates ran on this cycle. Like Schumer, Van Hollen has also served in Congress for decades.    Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate for nearly a decade, contends that he still has the needed votes to be elected majority leader. However, Van Hollen's challenge comes as a handful of current and incoming members have declined to back Schumer for the job.   Both sides still have time to shore up votes, with leadership elections set for early December.

title: Project Gryffindor: Meta's plan to get more school kids using Instagram
description: An aerial view of Meta headquarters on J
body:
An aerial view of Meta headquarters on Jan. 29, 2025 in Menlo Park, Calif.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   Internal Meta documents show the company planned to boost Instagram use among teens by targeting schools in an initiative it named "Project Gryffindor."   The project focused on growing what it called "school communities" in the U.S. by encouraging teens to include their school banner on their profiles and establishing a student directory that allows users to see and connect with others from their school who use the platform.   Meta launched the initiative in 2025, calling it a "school partnership program," and significantly expanded it in September 2026. The company said almost 17,000 schools had signed up for the program at the time.   
   Meta said the program sought to provide a safer experience on Instagram for children, including protecting them from bullying and online risks by allowing educators to report safety concerns to the company.   
   Another feature gives school-related accounts the ability to post stories and notes visible to all verified students and parents in a school community. Meta said these features would help students and parents stay informed about happenings at school. The announcement gave an example of a school using the Instagram Stories feature to share a notice of basketball tryouts.   However, in internal documents prior to the program's public launch, the company discussed more explicitly commercial motivations for establishing school networks. In a 2024 presentation on Project Gryffindor, Meta said that embedding in schools was a way to increase user "acquisition," "friending" and "invites" to join Instagram. Gryffindor is one of the four Hogwarts school houses from the Harry Potter books.   "We believe network connections will fuel organic and unattributed acquisition," the project's presentation states, referring to adding new users.   
   In another internal presentation from 2023, titled "Unlocking New Networks Through School Communities," Meta stated that its school program would "give teens a new reason to join / find more value in IG [Instagram]."   "Our current strategy of relying on power user teens to get less active friends onto IG may not be effective if there are full communities of teens that have not yet joined IG," the presentation stated.   The previously unreported Meta documents are part of evidence obtained by lawyers through discovery in a multidistrict lawsuit alleging that social media platforms are designed to be harmful to users under 18, and that the companies knew their products carried risks they failed to disclose. Meta, alongside TikTok, Google and Snap, are defendants in the cases, which were brought by children and their families, school districts and state attorneys general.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A cell phone locker is seen at Ronald McNair Sr. High School, Thursday, Aug. 7, 2025, in Atlanta.
                
                    Mike Stewart/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mike Stewart/Associated Press
    

   
   Online safety experts interviewed by NPR said that rather than boosting online safety, Instagram's school partnership program could make teen users more vulnerable to mental health issues and increase their likelihood of being targeted by predators.   
   "Meta's own documents refer to this very program as a mere way to get more teens addicted to Instagram and Facebook," said Sacha Haworth, the executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on tech policy. "Meta's latest attempt to trojan-horse their tech into the school day shows the business strategy remains the same: maximize their profits at our kids' expense."   According to Paul Raffile, a cybersecurity investigator, Instagram's school partnership program could create privacy and security vulnerabilities to teens' accounts that could be "a loophole that scammers, sextortion scammers, as well as groomers, would obviously exploit."   Using schools to recruit teen Instagram users   Meta has long focused on boosting Instagram's popularity among teenagers. The social media giant viewed the slowdown in teen Instagram user growth since TikTok's US launch in 2018 as "an existential threat for not just IG [Instagram] but the company overall," according to other internal documents submitted as evidence in the multidistrict lawsuit.   Internal documents show that as early as 2015, the company was making plans to form relationships with schools to acquire new teen users.   One company presentation from 2023 stated: "Our competitors in social connection are leveraging school integrations as a way to keep in touch with their community. Can we take things a step further and use school networks as a lever for acquisitions?" Snapchat also has a school and college community program, where users can apply to have their school badge displayed on their profile, which has faced criticism for facilitating inappropriate posts and bullying.   Another Meta document discussed how acquiring teen users would have the knock-on effect of introducing younger children to the platform. "Teens strongly influenced preteens' understanding of what and how frequently to share on Instagram," the document said. Meta's own policy states that Instagram users must be at least 13 years old to have an account.   
   In another internal Meta presentation focused on the long-term retention of users on Facebook, a bullet point stated: "Tweens (approximate age 10-12) are special. People who join Facebook as tweens have the highest long term retention out of all age groups." Facebook also has a minimum age requirement of 13 to use the platform.   Targeting schools may also have served as a strategy to increase the amount of time teens spent on Instagram. In a 2025 legal brieffiled on behalf of school districts and boards of education across the country, lawyers cited a 2015 internal comment from a Meta employee describing the company's engagement goals: "One of the things we need to optimize for is sneaking a look at your phone under your desk in the middle of Chemistry :)."   Meta targeted push notifications to students within specific schools, which it called "school blasts," the same legal brief states. The aim of these "blasts" was to "tip schools from inactive to active via network effects and incrementally increase teen MAP [monthly active persons] in those schools," the brief said.   The legal brief also outlined how the company developed the technical capability to determine when teen users were at school, "using location and school-specific information collected through data harvesting."   This contrasts with public statements Meta has made about teens' use of Instagram. "We don't want social media to be a distraction from school," the company said in its September 2026 announcement the school partnership program was expanding.   Meta spokesperson, Liza Crenshaw, said in a statement to NPR: "This story completely mischaracterizes a positive program that helps thousands of U.S. schools protect their students online, communicate with them safely about extracurricular activities, and easily report safety issues. In the past year, we've reviewed over 90% of bullying and harassment reports from participating schools within 48 hours. We don't want Instagram to be a distraction during class."   
   Through its Instagram Teen Accounts program, parents have been able to block their teens' access during the school day, since 2022, Crenshaw said.   Program could increase risk of predators targeting teens   Children participating in the school partnership program are verified by a third-party app and can display their school badge on their profile, which is visible to other teens they follow. "To help stay connected to classmates, students can see a directory of other students at their school, or make a school banner," Meta said in its September 2026 press release.   However, online safety experts interviewed by NPR say that rather than making teen users safer, the school partnership program could increase their vulnerability to being targeted by predators and scammers.   "This goes against all the internet safety training that parents and teachers have been trying to instill in their kids all these years," said John DeMay, whose 17-year-old son Jordan DeMay died by suicide in 2022 after being targeted in a sextortion blackmail scam on Instagram.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Instagram logo is seen on a cell phone in Boston, Oct. 14, 2022.
                
                    Michael Dwyer/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael Dwyer/Associated Press
    

   
   Teens in the U.S. are frequently targeted by sextortionists — scammers who typically pretend to be a romantic interest about the same age as their target, who then groom the teen and convince them to send sexually compromising photographs of themselves. Once the pictures are sent, the scammers reveal themselves to be blackmailers, threatening to send the pictures to their victims' contacts if they don't comply with their requests for money.   Many victims are teen boys, dozens of whom have died by suicide because of their victimization by sextortionists, according to the National Center of Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC).   One of the first pieces of information scammers want to extract from their victim is where they go to school, said Raffile. Because scammers often pose as teenagers online themselves, they would be able to see their victim's school banner if the victim starts to follow them on Instagram.   
   Identifying where a victim goes to school is "actually written into the script that the scammers use," he said. "Later on, when it comes time for the blackmail, they will use that information, threaten to send it to everybody in the school. They will find teachers and coaches at the school and threaten to send this content to them."   While Meta uses a third-party to verify students' email addresses before they are admitted into their school's partnership program, the student's accounts could easily be breached, experts said.   "There's nothing to say that you know a student's account can't get hacked and then taken by a criminal and then used for all sorts of nefarious purposes, whether it be sextortion, grooming," said Raffile. "Once an account is embedded within a school and has an active school profile, they can see all sorts of things like directories of the different clubs, different groups on campus, and that's a sextortionist's dream."   Teen Instagram accounts are often targets of hacking and security breaches, which can include social engineering and account takeover schemes, child safety advocates and experts said.   In one case, in February 2026, an online child predator hijacked hundreds of young people's social media accounts, including Instagram and Snapchat, before threatening to release sexually explicit images, according to a Department of Justice announcement.   "Facebook and Instagram and most of these social media platforms are not secure. They do not have enough security measures in place to keep the bad actors out. As we know, how easy it is for literally anybody, even a child, a 10-year-old child, to go and create an account and start using it," DeMay said. "Bad actors and adult criminals can do the same thing."   Meta did not provide a response to NPR about sextortion and cybersecurity concerns.   Partnership claims disputed by education nonprofit   In a September 2026 press release, Meta said its School Partnership Program was developed "in partnership" with the International Society for Technology in Education and the Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development (ISTE+ASCD), an education nonprofit.   
   ISTE+ASCD disputed the characterization that it is a partner on the project, and said it undertook "contract work" for the project to develop a process for educators to report inappropriate posts and accounts. That work concluded in 2025, the organization said.   When asked by NPR why Meta referred to ISTE+ASCD as a partner on its school partnership program a year after their contract concluded, Crenshaw said: "We were proud to work with ISTE on the initial development of the School Partnership Program."   Crenshaw said the program has since evolved and "ISTE has not been part of that work."   Both Meta and ISTE told NPR that ISTE initially reached out to Meta.   "School leaders had been telling us they needed more options to remove disruptive posts and accounts on Instagram," said ISTE spokesperson Daniel Obregon. "We shared that feedback with Meta and were contracted to help collect educator feedback and test the new [account reporting] functionality in schools."   This year, Meta has settled and lost several lawsuits alleging its products are harmful to children.   In August 2026, Meta agreed to a settlement worth up to $17.1 billion to resolve claims brought by dozens of state attorneys general alleging that Facebook and Instagram were designed to encourage compulsive use among children and teenagers and that the company misled the public about the risks. As part of the settlement, Meta denied the allegations against it.   In a landmark trial in Los Angeles in March 2026, a jury found that co-defendants YouTube and Meta designed their platforms to be addictive to young users. Meta also lost a two-phase lawsuit brought by the New Mexico attorney general, in which a jury found the company had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms and knowingly harmed children. Meta is appealing the verdict.   "How irresponsible for a company who has just been held liable in multiple lawsuits across the U.S. for intentionally harming teens and putting their privacy and safety at risk," said Raffile. "Now they're trying to get embedded into the schools.

title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
description: Families look on as President Donald Tru
body:
Families look on as President Donald Trump speaks during a ceremony to sign the "Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act" in the East Room of the White House on July 16, 2025.
                
                    Evan Vucci/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Evan Vucci/AP
    

   
   When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.   
   But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.    "The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.     Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.   
   What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.    "Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."   Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths   According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said.  By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.   
   Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.   "It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.   Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.   
   Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Joe Biden met China's President President Xi Jinping in Woodside, Calif., in November 2023, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperative conference. China agreed to curtail shipments of the chemicals used to make fentanyl, the drug at the heart of the U.S. overdose epidemic.
                
                    Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times
    

   
   The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.   Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.    White House on Biden role in declines   NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden.  In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.   "While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.    
   Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."    According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.   "We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated  operations," she said.   
   But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.   
   "I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."   Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.   Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.     The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.   "Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

schema.headline: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Her victory gives Democrats 56 senators in the upcoming Congress. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola secured a majority of first-place votes, eliminating the need for ranked-choice calculations. Her win flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. The race's final days were tumultuous due to allegations that Peltola's team tried to recruit another candidate to the race to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied any involvement.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mary Peltola looks on during a campaign rally at the Alaska Aviation Museum on October 30, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   Trump has arrived in the Southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he is set to meet with China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday. This will mark the third time these two leaders have met this year. They are expected to discuss trade, investment and tariffs, which are currently on hold.   🎧 The meeting is about establishing a tone, as the U.S. and China have agreed to have constructive strategic stability, NPR's Jennifer Pak tells Up First. The two leaders will later be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting. The trio may discuss a peace deal for Russia's war in Ukraine, but China says that Europe must be included. Pak says China wants to show that a world leader won't make decisions without input from smaller countries. This is especially significant, Pak says, because these meetings take place on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), where many smaller nations seek a voice in regional matters.   
   Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in an earnings call yesterday that the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct," according to Jones. Huang acknowledged he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency. The board unanimously accepted his resignation. Earlier yesterday, Huang said he would return as CEO if the board permitted it and agreed to testify before Congress regarding national security issues surrounding the company.   🎧 NPR's John Ruwitch said that Jones clearly wanted to dispel rumors, and showed support for interim CEO Colette Kress. He said she "has been at the center of the company's extraordinary growth." Kress also participated in the call, maintaining a business-as-usual demeanor, Ruwitch says. Nvidia posted revenue exceeding $115 billion for the quarter, which isn't surprising, as the numbers were secured before Huang's recent departure. Tech analyst Gaurav Gupta from Gartner tells Ruwitch that any impact from new leadership won't be reflected in the numbers for several months. Jones said the board would try to decide on a permanent CEO as soon as possible without rushing the decision.   
   Major organizations have been experiencing widespread crashes of computer and online systems. Apple reported significant outages yesterday, and the U.S. National Security Agency also experienced a breakdown. As of this morning, no major disruptions seem to be occurring. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that these incidents are related to one another or involve a malign actor or cybercriminal.   🎧 Cyber experts tell NPR's Greg Myre that artificial intelligence is uncovering previously undetected software flaws at an unprecedented pace. Companies are racing to patch or upgrade to address these vulnerabilities, but working under tight deadlines often leads to mistakes. As many systems undergo upgrades, people should anticipate disruptions along the way, Myre says. However, the optimistic perspective is that computer networks are expected to become more robust and resilient within the next year or two due to the improvements.   Deep dive   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Kratom and related 7-OH products are widely available at gas stations, smoke shops, liquor stores and online. As early as Friday, the federal government could make some of the products illegal.
                
                    Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images
    

   
   In recent years, highly concentrated products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) have emerged online and at smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. These products, available as tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolates, contain one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom. Unlike kratom leaf products, 7-OH acts more like an opioid in the human brain. Some people use kratom to maintain long-term recovery from opioid addiction. Others say it helps them feel energized or focused. Users of 7-OH and kratom can show signs of addiction, and unclear product labeling makes it hard to determine the quantities consumed. Over the past decade, the U.S. government has tried to restrict these products, but public opposition has kept them legal. Recently, this situation has started to change.   ➡️ In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration restricted the manufacture and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids from 7-OH and other related compounds. They were classified under the Controlled Substances Act alongside drugs like heroin and LSD.➡️ Kratom advocates were concerned that new rules would impact products with "trace amounts" of the opioid MGPI. The American Kratom Association filed a federal lawsuit against the DEA on Aug. 26, seeking to keep natural kratom products with MGPI legal.➡️ On Oct. 9, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI, leading the DEA to revise its stance to focus on restricting products with higher concentrations of these substances.➡️ Opponents of the restriction argue that the products helped them avoid traditional opioids. Some point to the decrease in opioid deaths in the U.S.➡️ The National Institute on Drug Abuse says that early studies indicate kratom and its compounds deserve more exploration as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder.   
   Real Talk With a Doc   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR
    

   
   Family physician Mara Gordon answers reader health questions monthly for NPR's special series Real Talk with a Doc. Send in your question to thrive@npr.org.   Artificial intelligence scribes help doctors take notes in various settings, from gynecologist visits to emergency rooms. Dr. Gordon says the technology saves time and allows her to focus entirely on her patients without the distraction of multitasking. But she also understands why patients might feel uneasy about new technology, and says she shares their concerns about privacy. Here's what Dr. Gordon says you should know about AI scribes:   🩺 The scribe uses "automatic speech recognition" technology to record the conversation between the doctor and the patient. After the visit, the recording is transcribed and turned into a medical note of the exam's findings and the doctor's decisions.🩺 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance is crucial for AI scribe services to ensure they protect patient privacy. Software companies must safeguard data by encrypting it, controlling access and implementing systems to prevent data breaches. Most companies delete recorded conversations after a specified period.🩺 AI scribes can make mistakes, which is why doctors must review AI-generated notes before signing them and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software requires doctors to sign a user agreement, making them liable for all content in the medical record.🩺Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates have raised concerns that this could widen health disparities.🩺 You can always opt out of using an AI scribe during your doctor's visit. But opting out of AI in medicine more broadly could be tricky.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A selection of different flavored manoushe.
                
                    Jawad Rizkallah

   NPR's Breakfast Around the World series is spotlighting Lebanon's man'ouché, a beloved breakfast flatbread. It's a U.N.-certified part of intangible cultural heritage, with a unique twist crafted by generations of Lebanese.The Pan American Health Organization announced yesterday that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status. It is now considered endemic because a strain has persisted in the country for more than a year.The oldest survivor of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Freeman Johnson, died this weekend at his Cape Cod home at the age of 106.   
   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: She retired early to care for family. New work rules for food aid disrupted that
description: Lisa Reese sits with her granddaughter,
body:
Lisa Reese sits with her granddaughter, Dallas Medley, 2, in the Capitol Heights, Md. home they share with Reese's daughter and uncle.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   CAPITOL HEIGHTS, Md. – Over nearly four decades of working — at a liquor store, cleaning apartments and in hospitality — Lisa Reese never received government assistance. Now, after her decision to retire at 62 and apply for SNAP food aid, her plans to take care of family members in need became complicated.   It felt like the right time to retire, she said, sitting on the front porch of a gray clapboard house in Maryland, just outside Washington, D.C. The home has been in the family since her grandparents owned it, and three generations live here now. Her 2-year-old granddaughter peeks through the front door.   
   Reese spent the past 25 years at Marriott, where working at the front desk, in room service, and at events meant "there was no sitting down … I was tired!" she said with a soft laugh. But more than that, she chose to retire because she was needed at home.   
   Her 80-year-old mother is in senior living and Reese visits often. She shares the house with her uncle, who's had surgery for liver cancer, as well as her daughter and granddaughter, whom she helps care for. "Daycare was expensive," she said. "So I decided to retire to take care of everybody. I don't know if that's crazy."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Lisa Reese stands outside the home that's been in the family since her grandparents owned it, and where three generations still live.  She decided to retire early to help care for her uncle and granddaughter.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   Reese's daughter also gets SNAP and is exempt from the work rule since her child is young — but she has a job in childcare. There's also a waiver for those who care for someone incapacitated, but Reese's uncle is not.   After leaving her job, getting by mainly on Social Security was tough. The price of everything seemed to go up this year, especially the gas bill which "went through the roof," she said. "One of my bills was $500. Five hundred!"   She scrimped as much as she could, stuck to a tight budget, and went to a nearby food bank. But it wasn't enough.   
   This summer, Reese was approved for a small amount from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as SNAP. But to get $63 a month in food aid, she must work, train or volunteer for 80 hours a month.   That requirement is part of sweeping changes and cuts to both SNAP and Medicaid in the One Big Beautiful Bill that President Trump signed last year. It slashed funding and expanded work rules, including for people aged 55 to 64.   Some 5 million people nationwide have lost federal food benefits since then, estimates the left-leaning Center for Budget and Policy Priorities. Newly empowered Democrats want to roll back the changes, but Trump administration officials have said repeatedly that they are helping to tackle waste, fraud and abuse.   "People are being punished"   Not far from where Reese lives, the nonprofit Mission of Love Charities has been swamped with need this year. It serves people who are homeless or low-income, and had to reduce food pantry visits from once a week to every other week. It also hired a third case worker to help people sign up for SNAP and Medicaid, and connect them with housing and jobs.   "We see it every day, people get cut off" from food aid, said CEO Adenia Bradley. Sometimes it's for red tape or a small error, sometimes people lose benefits because of the new work rules.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mission of Love Charities CEO Adenia Bradley, left, talks with volunteer Lisa Reese. Reese's volunteer work fulfills the SNAP work requirements that were expanded last year to include older adults aged 55 to 64.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   Maryland has tried to make it less complicated for people to get and stay on SNAP. It's created one application for multiple benefits that works on a smartphone, and made it easier and quicker to verify eligibility to renew the program. The decline in enrollment has been less sharp here than in some other states. And when officials do inform people their aid is being cut off, they connect them immediately with a job assistance center. "They say that you have this appointment at this time. If you need to reschedule, call this number," said case worker Brooke Wright.   
   But the labor market is still tough. "One of our volunteers, she did three work applications already and she cannot find a job yet," said case worker Jatmna Cabrera.   
   Bradley has allowed a few people to meet the new work requirements by volunteering at the Mission. They include Lisa Reese.   On a recent day, in a corner of the high-ceilinged warehouse, she filled crinkly bags with food for people who would line up later to pick them up. "Snacks, water, drinks and they get two sandwiches," Reese said.   Her four-hour shift is in the morning, so she can still watch her granddaughter in the afternoons. And she loves helping people this way. "I feel better when they walk past and they wave at me, "Hey, Miss Mission of Love!" she said. "It makes me feel good that they're eating."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mission of Love Charities volunteer Lisa Reese packs snack bags for unhoused and low-income clients. She also enrolled in Medicaid after retiring, and new work rules for that program kick in next year.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   But CEO Bradley can only let so many people volunteer here, and she worries the need will only grow. "So now we are researching places for people to volunteer, other than us, so we can give them referrals," she said.   She noted the expanded work rules apply to people who had long been exempt from them: Able-bodied older adults, parents of adolescents, veterans, homeless people and some noncitizens including refugees.   "I'm always for a case-by-case basis, but what they're doing now is lumping them all in one pot," she said. Certainly for older people, she does not think a blanket work rule makes sense. "I think people are being punished for being on the help that the government has said" someone is qualified for, she said. "They don't deserve that."   In a statement to NPR the Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, said "an expectation to work, train, or volunteer for 20 hours per week, as few as four hours per day, is not punishment. Industriousness and contribution to community should be applauded, not used as scare tactics." And on calls to roll back the rules, the USDA said, "Democrats and their pervasive advocacy arm have never met a welfare program they don't want to bloat, overfund, or exploit."   
   President Trump's larger approach to tackle waste, fraud and abuse "has brought down costs significantly," said White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster in a statement to NPR. As for SNAP specifically, "the program's mission to be temporary help for those in tough times was a total failure, but President Trump's historic legislation began the process to halt fraud and ensure that it only serves eligible Americans who need it most," she said.   Lisa Reese agrees that SNAP use should only be temporary.   "The ones that's been on it for 10, 15, 20 years, yeah, they do need to get off of it. It's hurting folks like me," she said. "I'm sorry if that sounds cruel. But go after them, not the retirees."   Reese will soon face a double whammy. Since retiring, she's been on Medicaid, and new work rules for that program kick in next year. But she isn't sure she can keep up volunteering 80 hours a month.   "I have arthritis in my hand real bad. My thighs hurt so bad, and sciatica, high blood pressure, you name it," she said.   Her thinking now is to get off SNAP and Medicaid if, hopefully, she can find a part-time job to pay for a private health plan. She and her daughter are researching plans they could split the cost of. It could be another hit to her budget, but only until she turns 65. Then she could fully retire, and spend more time helping out family, like she hoped to be doing now.

title: Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
description: China's President Xi Jinping, center, st
body:
China's President Xi Jinping, center, stands as President Trump, left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, Wednesday.
                
                    Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press via AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press via AP
    

   
   SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.   
   Trump's meeting with Putin would be the first time that the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia's war in Ukraine.   
   Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin as relations between the United States and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.   The U.S. official who confirmed the Trump-Putin meeting in China spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to share plans that were not yet public.   The exact timing of the meeting on Thursday was unclear. Trump already had public plans for a separate meeting with Xi and a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin.   
   Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin in their joint meeting about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.   Before the trip, Trump's aides told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at the APEC CEO summit held ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, southern China's Guangdong province on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026.
                
                    Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin
    

   
   "I think it's very close to getting it done," the Republican president said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."   Trump lands in China's tech hub as outages cause concerns at home   Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America's status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the U.S. public.   The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.   As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the U.S. worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.   
   "It's fine," Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."   But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.   At the start of the second day of Trump's trip, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. Rubio told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages were connected or were tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.   "Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.   Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Trump walks with China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen, in southern China's Guangdong Province, Wednesday.
                
                    Mark Schiefelbein/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Schiefelbein/AP
    

   
   Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, reciprocating a gesture by the American leader during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.   Trump and Xi greeted each other on Wednesday at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as a group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier in the day, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their long-standing friendship.   Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.   
   As leaders were introduced on Wednesday night before an APEC group photo, Putin approached Trump. They shook hands and traded greetings.   The White House said Trump was scheduled earlier Wednesday to have separate meetings with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.   Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos   Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.   Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and he complimented Trump for "working very hard."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, walks beside U.S. President Donald Trump during a welcome ceremony marking Trump's state visit to the Philippines at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026.
                
                    Aaron Favila/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Aaron Favila/AP
    

   
   Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.   "Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."   He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached.   Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the country's former first lady who is the mother of the Philippines' current president. Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene.   What's on the agenda for Trump's meetings with Xi and Putin   The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease because Trump has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.   His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.   
   Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.   The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.   Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.

title: How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
description: Dick Walsh won a championship tournament
body:
Dick Walsh won a championship tournament at East Potomac Park in 1923.
                
                    Library of Congress
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Library of Congress
    

   
   Runners and cyclists still have access to D.C.'s East Potomac Park, despite the Trump administration's plans to close it over the weekend. But its golf course is conspicuously missing the flags that typically mark the holes — and at least some of the people who typically play them.   Federal Judge Ana Reyes issued a restraining order late Saturday to keep the beloved park open for two weeks, just hours before the National Park Service planned to cut off public access to most of it indefinitely.   But Sunday marked the last day of the government's lease with the National Links Trust, which had operated the golf course since 2020. And Reyes did not order the government to keep operating the golf course — though she has since signaled she may consider it.   
   "Whether and how Defendants do so is solely within their discretion, but Defendants cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course," Reyes wrote in her 30-page order.   Reyes criticized the government's "pretextual" justification and "arbitrary" timeline for closing the park, which she said would "irreparably harm" the people who enjoy it on a daily basis — including the local preservationists and golfers who first sued to protect the course in February.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Protesters gathered at East Potomac Park on Sunday to rally against its planned closure.
                
                    Tom Brenner/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/AP
    

   
   In comments on social media and to the press, President Trump slammed her decision and said his administration will appeal. The White House referred NPR to those comments.   "What she's done is she stopped it for 15 days," Trump told reporters when asked about the case on Monday. "You can't stop that."   The National Park Service and Interior Department did not respond to NPR's questions about the future of the course.   
   Trump has his sights set on redeveloping the golf course — which he has repeatedly decried as decrepit and dangerous — into a championship-level venue. Administration officials are due to present that vision to the federal Commission of Fine Arts on Thursday.   According to the government's 64-page submission, architect Tom Fazio's design would replace East Potomac's three courses of varying difficulty levels with one 18-hole layout stretching across almost the entire peninsula.   The plan is broadly unpopular in D.C., as it would eliminate the perimeter road beloved by runners and cyclists, and the grassy areas where people picnic and birdwatch. Critics worry the new course would be less accessible for beginners and less affordable for everyone. Prices currently range from $17 to $48 per round, and the Trump administration has not said what a round at the new course would cost, only that locals would be able to play at a discount.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The proposed redesign, which the Trump administration has submitted to federal arts commissions for review, shows one 18-hole course stretching across East Potomac Park. It would replace the park's three existing courses for different skill levels and eliminate the road around the perimeter.
                
                    Department of the Interior
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Department of the Interior
    

   
   Locals agree that East Potomac could use some improvements, including to its long-eroded seawall. But that's very different from overhauling the course entirely. Reyes pressed government lawyers at a Friday hearing on why the National Park Service chose the latter.   
   Officials pointed to Trump's social media directives, but also argued that the park needs to be closed for other reasons: to repair the seawall (for which it acknowledged Friday there is no plan yet) and because of the lack of a golf course operator (a situation Reyes described as "entirely self-inflicted"). And it says there are nearby recreational areas people can use instead — though critics say there is no substitute. Reyes seemed to agree.   "Plaintiffs' harms are tied to 'East Potomac's beauty, historic layout, and historic designs,'" Reyes wrote. "While there are other parks in Washington, D.C., there is no other East Potomac Park."   The East Potomac golf course is known for its history of accessibility    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                East Potomac Park, as seen from above in 1935, is home not only to a golf course but also to grassy picnic areas and a perimeter road beloved by runners and cyclists.
                
                    Library of Congress
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Library of Congress
    

   
   East Potomac is a man-made peninsula, originally dredged from the Potomac River to facilitate shipping channels. Congress designated the land a public park in 1897, declaring it should be "forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people." It houses many forms of recreation, including a tennis complex, a perimeter road and a 220-acre golf course.   The golf course at East Potomac is one of seven that the federal government built in D.C. between 1917 and 1948, according to a 2017 National Park Service historical report. It calls that "a testament to the rise in popularity of the sport of golf and the demand for public golf courses for those who could not [afford] private memberships to exclusive golf clubs in the early decades of the 20th century."   That number has since dwindled to three. East Potomac is the busiest, especially after a renewed interest in golf during the COVID-19 pandemic: It hosted some 125,000 rounds of golf in 2025 alone.   "In a city where politicians are constantly focused on what separates us, East Potomac is one of the few remaining spaces where no matter who you are, what you do, or the state of your game, everyone is welcome and everyone is treated the same," plaintiff Dave Roberts said in a statement when the lawsuit was first filed.   
   Its first 18 holes were designed by Walter Travis, one of the top amateur golfers in the U.S., who shaped dozens of courses during the "golden age of golf" (which ended around the onset of the Great Depression).   He modeled East Potomac after Scottish "links-style" courses, which are known for their coastal terrain and relative lack of trees — in this case offering clear views of the Potomac River and the Washington Monument. And, in a unique twist, Travis designed the course to be reversible, for the durability of the grounds and to the delight of those who played them.   "Travis captured a design style that characterized the era's greatest courses, including East Potomac: difficult for aggressive elite players, yet playable for unskilled beginners," plaintiffs wrote in their February complaint.   The first portion of the course opened to the public in July 1920. It cost 25 cents to play a round, including locker room privileges. The course was a huge hit, drawing 16,345 golfers in its first year. That number nearly quadrupled by 1921, according to the National Park Service.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Golfers play in a tournament at East Potomac in June 1923.

        Library of Congress
    

   
   The links grew to meet demand over the next decade, ultimately expanding into three courses (red, white and blue) plus one of the first miniature golf courses in the U.S., which features tiny replicas of the White House and U.S. Capitol and is now the country's oldest continually operating mini-golf course.   But despite its broad appeal, East Potomac initially allowed Black players access only during limited hours one day per week. A separate course, Langston, opened to serve Black residents in 1939 — on the site of a former city dump — but suffered from neglect and downright hazardous conditions.   One day in June 1941, three Black golfers showed up at East Potomac and demanded to play.   According to historical accounts, they had a "fair-skinned" friend purchase their tickets but were turned away. They returned with some powerful government allies, and park police ruled that the men should be allowed to play since they had tickets. The trio completed 18 holes, accompanied by police and amidst the "boos and chorus of insults" from white onlookers.   
   The next day, the interior secretary issued an order opening the course to all players, regardless of race.   
   Harassment and other forms of segregation persisted at the city's municipal courses for over a decade, but the golfers' 1941 protest is seen as a turning point in the fight for equal access to public spaces. The National Park Service says it "opened the door for the full integration of all national park facilities in 1945."   Judge Reyes has nodded to that part of the park's history throughout the case, including while grilling government lawyers at a mid-October hearing.   "We're not just talking about some putt-putt thing that went up by the beach you take your kids to," she said, adding that the course holds a rich history and "deep amount of meaning" to locals. "There was bravery in the people who first desegregated this golf course."   The course has only closed — temporarily — a few times in its history, including for a portion of World War II and for a few days after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, in 1968, when National Guard troops responding to riots set up camp at East Potomac.   What would change?    There have been changes at East Potomac over the decades, like the addition of a two-tiered driving range in the 1990s.   But, as the National Park Service said in its 2017 report, the city's courses continue their original intent "to allow golfers of all ages and skill levels to play at an [affordable] cost compared to private and even semi-private clubs in the area and remain extremely popular."   Plaintiffs note in their lawsuit that a weekend round at East Potomac's blue course costs $48, compared to $89 for a Sunday morning round at the Laurel Hill Golf Club, a municipal golf course in nearby Fairfax County, Va.   
   Critics worry a championship-style course would be even less affordable — especially one that Trump described over the weekend this way: "All over the World it will be acclaimed as being the Best Golf Course anywhere."   Trump said locals will get a 50% discount. But the administration has not said how much it will cost to play. The administration's proposal only points to "benchmark" championship courses in California, Texas and New York, where locals pay up to $90 per weekend round, even with a discount. The government admitted Friday that those were merely illustrations.   
   There's also the question of how beginner-friendly the redesigned course would be.

   Reyes pointed out last week that under the administration's proposal, even from the shortest tee at every hole, the course adds up to 6,013 yards. She asked the government how that compares to recommended course length averages for different types of players, including seniors and young players, and did not get an answer.   The administration said repeatedly that its plan is not yet final, as it still needs to undergo various federal reviews that require input from experts and the public. Lawyers told Reyes that there is no contract between the government and Fazio, the architect — despite Trump's repeated social media posts saying work would begin on Nov. 15.   Even so, the government said it had to close the park that day in part because there was no one left to run the course.   The nonprofit National Links Trust had entered into a 50-year lease to operate the city's municipal golf courses in 2020. But the government terminated its East Potomac lease last December, accusing it of failing to make capital improvements. The trust continued to manage the course on an interim basis — and still manages the city's other courses — but announced last month that its role would end at East Potomac on Nov. 15.   Reyes said that timing was no coincidence.   "[The National Park Service] claims that it would be unable to safely manage the course itself. In other words, the Government's hands are tied," she wrote in her order. "But the Government tied the knot itself."   
   Reyes has been openly hesitant to take the administration at its word at this point in the increasingly inflammatory case. She ordered an inquiry into potential misconduct by government lawyers and officials after they cut down hundreds of trees on short notice in October and repeatedly contradicted the president's social media announcements in court.   At Friday's hearing, Reyes questioned why the National Park Service couldn't renew its lease with the operator, especially since it has already entrusted it to manage two other municipal golf courses for another 50 years. She mulled whether the government could theoretically step in to run the golf course, at least until it finds another party to do so.   
   Reyes appears to be weighing whether she has the legal authority to compel the Trump administration to do that. On Monday, she ordered both parties to submit briefings discussing "whether the Court may require the Government to operate East Potomac Golf Course in order to maintain the status quo."

schema.headline: How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
